title: Advanced Diagnostic Techniques
subtopics: Reducing a failure to a minimal reproducible case
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of advanced diagnostic techniques.
Choose and interpret a suitable Docker example connected to advanced diagnostic techniques.
Predict an expected result and verify it using observable evidence in a controlled environment.

content.intro: This lesson covers Advanced Diagnostic Techniques. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: Troubleshoot from evidence: reproduce the failure, identify the affected container/service, collect logs and inspect configuration/state, test one hypothesis at a time, then verify both the fix and a relevant failure case. Avoid broad cleanup or permission changes that hide the cause. Learning advanced diagnostic techniques helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

items.title: Container inspection
items.text: For container inspection, name the relevant Docker object, setting, or operational step; predict its effect; and capture evidence from a controlled test or inspection command. Relate the result back to advanced diagnostic techniques rather than assuming that a successful command proves the wider system is correct.

items.title: Network inspection
items.text: A network creates a connectivity boundary. Inspect the network and its attached endpoints, and test from the source service rather than assuming host connectivity proves container connectivity.

items.title: Docker daemon logs
items.text: The daemon/API executes requests against an Engine endpoint. Access should be limited because an unrestricted daemon can usually control host-level resources.

items.title: Docker events
items.text: Operational signals should help answer what failed, when it failed, and what changed. Establish a baseline and record the checks used to decide that the service recovered.

items.title: Resource statistics
items.text: Measure the workload under a repeatable baseline and change one variable at a time. Resource options and observed enforcement can differ by platform.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with the supplied example for advanced diagnostic techniques. Before running it, state what you expect to happen. Compare the real output with that prediction, then change one variable or setting in a disposable lab to test the boundary of the idea. If a command is not supported on your operating system or installed Docker version, consult the linked official reference and record the actual version rather than guessing.

task: Apply advanced diagnostic techniques to a small local case. Record the configuration or command, expected result, observed result, one limitation/edge case, and how you verified the result.
hints: Begin with read-only inspection commands and identify the active Docker context before any mutating action.
Use a disposable name, local test image, and synthetic data; change one thing at a time.
If the outcome differs, preserve the exact error and logs, check the official reference for your installed version, and document the verified fix.
expected_output: Version information plus local container and image listings; the commands help identify the starting state for a focused lab.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
